title: Sum and Average
prompt: Given the array {4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42}, write a C program that prints the sum of the numbers and their average with 2 decimal places.
hint: Loop with a for loop and keep a running total. To avoid integer division, cast the sum to double before dividing. Use %.2f in printf.

title: FizzBuzz
prompt: Print the numbers 1 to 15, one per line. For multiples of 3 print "Fizz" instead, for multiples of 5 print "Buzz", and for multiples of both print "FizzBuzz".
output:
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz
hint: Use the % (modulo) operator: i % 3 == 0 means i is a multiple of 3. Check the "both" case (i % 15 == 0) first, or it will never be reached.

title: Temperature Table
prompt: Print a Celsius-to-Fahrenheit table from 0 to 100 in steps of 20. Formula: F = C × 9 / 5 + 32. Show Fahrenheit with 1 decimal place.
hint: A for loop can count by 20: for (int c = 0; c <= 100; c += 20). Write 9.0 instead of 9 so the math is done with decimals.

title: Max and Min
prompt: Find the largest and smallest values in the array {12, -7, 45, 3, 0, 29} using a single loop.
hint: Start both max and min at the first element (not at 0, which breaks with negative numbers), then compare every other element against them.

title: Count Evens and Odds
prompt: Count how many even and how many odd numbers are in the array {3, 8, 11, 14, 20, 7, 6}.
hint: A number is even when n % 2 == 0. Keep two counters and increase one of them on each loop iteration.

title: Factorial
prompt: Write a function unsigned long long factorial(int n) that uses a loop (not recursion). Print 0!, 5!, 10! and 20!.
hint: Start with result = 1 and multiply by 2, 3, ... n. 20! is huge, so you need unsigned long long and the %llu format. Remember 0! is 1.

title: Digit Counter
prompt: For n = 98765, count how many digits it has and add them up. Do it with math, not by converting to a string.
hint: n % 10 gives you the last digit. n / 10 (integer division) removes it. Repeat while n > 0.

title: Fibonacci Sequence
prompt: Print the first 10 Fibonacci numbers on one line, separated by spaces. Each number is the sum of the two before it, starting 0, 1.
hint: Keep two variables a and b. Each step: print a, then compute next = a + b, shift a = b and b = next. Print a space before every number except the first.

title: Reverse a Number
prompt: Write int reverse(int n) that reverses the digits of a positive number, so 12345 becomes 54321. Test it with 12345 and 1200.
hint: Build the answer digit by digit: rev = rev * 10 + n % 10, then n /= 10. Notice what happens to the zeros in 1200.

title: Linear Search
prompt: Write int find(const int arr[], int n, int target) that returns the index of target in the array, or -1 if it isn't there. Use the array {7, 2, 9, 4, 1} and search for 9 and 5.
hint: Loop from index 0 to n - 1 and return i as soon as arr[i] == target. If the loop finishes without finding it, return -1.

title: Prime Numbers
prompt: Write int is_prime(int n) and use it to print every prime number from 2 to 50 on one line, separated by spaces.
hint: A number is prime if nothing from 2 up to its square root divides it evenly. Loop with d * d <= n so you don't need sqrt().

title: Count the Vowels
prompt: Count the vowels (a, e, i, o, u, upper or lower case) in the string "Programming in C is fun".
hint: A C string ends with the '\0' character, so loop until text[i] == '\0'. A switch statement with several case labels makes the vowel check tidy.

title: GCD and LCM
prompt: Write int gcd(int a, int b) using Euclid's algorithm, then int lcm(int a, int b) that uses it. Print both for 48 and 18.
hint: Euclid: while b isn't 0, replace (a, b) with (b, a % b). When b hits 0, a is the GCD. Then lcm = a / gcd(a, b) * b (dividing first avoids overflow).

title: Write Your Own strlen
prompt: Without using <string.h>, write int my_strlen(const char *s) that returns the length of a string. Test it on "hello", "" (empty) and "Pixel 11".
output:
"hello" has 5 chars
"" has 0 chars
"Pixel 11" has 8 chars
hint: Count characters until you hit the terminating '\0'. To print quote marks inside printf, escape them as \".

title: Swap with Pointers
prompt: Write void swap(int *a, int *b) that swaps two integers. Start with x = 3 and y = 7 and print them before and after calling swap(&x, &y).
output:
Before: x = 3, y = 7
After: x = 7, y = 3
hint: C passes arguments by value, so the function needs the addresses. Use *a to read or write the value a points to, and a temporary variable to hold one value.

title: Reverse an Array
prompt: Write void reverse(int arr[], int n) that reverses an array in place (no second array). Reverse {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and print it.
hint: Use two indexes: left starts at 0, right at n - 1. Swap arr[left] and arr[right], then move them toward each other until they meet.

title: Reverse a String
prompt: Write void reverse_str(char *s) that reverses a string in place. Reverse "Hello, C!" and print the result.
hint: Same two-index trick as reversing an array, but the right index starts at strlen(s) - 1. Declare the text as char text[] = "..." so it can be modified.

title: Palindrome Check
prompt: Write int is_palindrome(const char *s) that returns 1 if the word reads the same forwards and backwards. Test "racecar", "level" and "coding".
output:
racecar: palindrome
level: palindrome
coding: not a palindrome
hint: Compare s[i] with s[j] where i starts at the front and j at the back. If any pair differs, it's not a palindrome. You don't need to build a reversed copy.

title: Uppercase Converter
prompt: Without using toupper(), write void to_upper(char *s) that converts every lowercase letter to uppercase. Convert "hello, pixel 11!".
hint: Characters are just numbers. If c is between 'a' and 'z', then c - 'a' + 'A' is the uppercase version. Leave everything else alone.

title: Bubble Sort
prompt: Write void bubble_sort(int arr[], int n) and sort {64, 34, 25, 12, 22, 11, 90} in ascending order.
hint: Repeatedly walk the array and swap neighbours that are in the wrong order. After each pass the largest remaining value has "bubbled" to the end. Bonus: stop early if a pass made no swaps.

title: Print in Binary
prompt: Write void print_binary(unsigned int n) that prints a number in base 2. Print 0, 5, 13 and 255.
hint: n & 1 gives the lowest bit, and n >>= 1 shifts it away. That produces the bits backwards, so store them in a char array and print it in reverse. Handle 0 separately.

title: Count the 1 Bits
prompt: Write int count_bits(unsigned int n) that returns how many bits are set to 1. Test it on 0, 7, 10 and 255.
hint: Add n & 1 to a counter, then shift with n >>= 1, until n is 0. Bonus trick: n &= n - 1 clears the lowest 1 bit, so you can loop once per set bit.

title: Recursive Power
prompt: Write long long power(long long base, int exp) using recursion (no loops, no pow()). Print 2^10, 3^5 and 7^0.
hint: Every recursive function needs a base case: anything to the power 0 is 1. Otherwise base^exp = base * base^(exp - 1).

title: Binary Search
prompt: Write int binary_search(const int arr[], int n, int target) for a sorted array. Search {2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 56, 72, 91} for 23 and for 7.
hint: Keep lo and hi indexes. Check the middle: if it's too small, search the right half (lo = mid + 1); if too big, the left half (hi = mid - 1). Stop when lo > hi.

title: Letter Frequency
prompt: Count how many times each letter appears in "hello world". Print only the letters that appear, in alphabetical order.
hint: Use an array int counts[26] = {0}. For a lowercase letter c, its slot is counts[c - 'a']. Then loop 0..25 and print 'a' + i for any non-zero count.

title: Word Counter
prompt: Write int count_words(const char *s) that counts words separated by any number of spaces. Test it on "  C is   a powerful   language  " (note the extra spaces).
hint: Track whether you're currently inside a word. Count a new word only when you move from a space to a non-space character.

title: Matrix Multiplication
prompt: Multiply the 2×2 matrices A = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}} and B = {{5, 6}, {7, 8}} and print the result, one row per line.
hint: Each result cell C[i][j] is the sum of A[i][k] * B[k][j] for every k. That's three nested loops: i, j, then k. Start C at all zeros.

title: Dynamic Array
prompt: Use malloc to create an array of n = 6 ints. Fill it with the squares of 1 to n, print them on one line, then free the memory.
hint: malloc(n * sizeof(int)) returns a pointer you can index like an array. Always check it isn't NULL, and call free() when you're done.

title: Student Records
prompt: Define struct Student { char name[20]; int score; }. Make an array with Ana 88, Ben 95, Cleo 79 and Dev 91. Print the top student and the class average.
hint: Access fields with a dot: students[i].score. Track the index of the best student rather than copying the struct around.

title: Reverse a Linked List
prompt: Build a linked list 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 with malloc. Print it, reverse it in place, print it again, and free every node.
hint: To reverse, walk the list with three pointers: prev (starts NULL), the current node, and next. For each node, save next, point the node back at prev, then step forward.

title: Greeting with f-strings
prompt: Store name = "Ada" and age = 36 in variables. Use an f-string to print a greeting that also says how old she'll be next year.
output: Hi Ada! Next year you'll be 37.
hint: Put an f before the opening quote, then anything inside {curly braces} is evaluated, including math like {age + 1}.
solution:
name = "Ada"
age = 36

print(f"Hi {name}! Next year you'll be {age + 1}.")

title: Sum of Even Numbers
prompt: Add up all the even numbers from 1 to 100 using a for loop and print the total. Bonus: do it again in one line with sum() and range().
hint: range(1, 101) goes from 1 to 100. A number is even when n % 2 == 0. For the bonus, range() takes a third "step" argument.
solution:
total = 0
for n in range(1, 101):
    if n % 2 == 0:
        total += n
print(total)

# Bonus: one line
print(sum(range(2, 101, 2)))

title: Times Table
prompt: Print the 7 times table from 7 x 1 to 7 x 10, one line each, in the format "7 x 3 = 21".
hint: A for loop over range(1, 11) gives you 1 to 10. An f-string makes the formatting easy.

title: Count the Vowels
prompt: Write count_vowels(text) that returns how many vowels (a, e, i, o, u) are in a string, ignoring case. Test it on "Learning Python every day".
hint: Lower-case the text first with .lower(). The in operator works on strings: ch in "aeiou" is True for a vowel.

title: Largest Without max()
prompt: Find the largest number in [3, 41, 12, 9, 74, 15] without using the built-in max() function.
hint: Assume the first item is the largest, then loop over the rest and replace it whenever you see something bigger.

title: List Comprehension
prompt: In a single line, build a list of the squares of the even numbers from 1 to 10, then print it.
hint: A list comprehension looks like [expression for item in iterable if condition].
solution:
squares = [n * n for n in range(1, 11) if n % 2 == 0]
print(squares)

title: Palindrome Checker
prompt: Write is_palindrome(word) that ignores upper/lower case. Test it on "level", "python" and "Racecar".
output:
level -> True
python -> False
Racecar -> True
hint: The slice word[::-1] gives you the string reversed. Compare the lower-cased word to its reverse.

title: Temperature Converter
prompt: Write c_to_f(celsius) that returns Fahrenheit rounded to 1 decimal place (F = C × 9 / 5 + 32). Convert [0, 25, 37, 100] and print the new list.
hint: round(value, 1) rounds to one decimal place. Then use a list comprehension to apply the function to every temperature.

title: Word Frequency
prompt: Count how many times each word appears in "the cat and the hat and the bat" using a dictionary. Print each word and its count in the order the words first appear.
hint: .split() breaks a sentence into words. counts.get(word, 0) returns 0 for words you haven't seen yet. Dictionaries remember insertion order.

title: Remove Duplicates
prompt: Write unique(items) that removes duplicates from a list but keeps the original order. Test it on [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 5, 2].
hint: list(set(items)) loses the order. Instead, keep a set of items you've already seen and only append an item the first time.

title: Find the Missing Number
prompt: The list [3, 7, 1, 2, 8, 4, 5] holds the numbers 1 to 8 with exactly one missing. Find it without sorting.
hint: The sum of 1..n is n × (n + 1) / 2. Subtract the sum of the list from that and you're left with the missing number.
solution:
nums = [3, 7, 1, 2, 8, 4, 5]
n = len(nums) + 1

expected = n * (n + 1) // 2
missing = expected - sum(nums)
print("Missing:", missing)

title: Longest Word
prompt: Find the longest word in "Practice makes progress every single day". If two words tie, keep the first one. Print the word and its length.
hint: max() takes a key= argument: max(words, key=len) compares words by length. When there's a tie it returns the first one.
solution:
sentence = "Practice makes progress every single day"

longest = max(sentence.split(), key=len)
print(f"Longest: {longest} ({len(longest)} letters)")

title: Prime Numbers
prompt: Write is_prime(n), then use it in a list comprehension to print every prime number below 30.
hint: You only need to test divisors up to the square root: range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1). Numbers below 2 are not prime.

title: Second Largest
prompt: Find the second largest distinct value in [10, 4, 10, 7, 9] in a single pass (no sorting).
hint: Track two variables, first and second. When you find a new largest, the old largest becomes second. Skip values equal to first. The quick way to check your answer: sorted(set(nums))[-2].

title: Anagram Check
prompt: Write is_anagram(a, b) that ignores spaces and case. Test ("listen", "silent"), ("hello", "world") and ("Dormitory", "dirty room").
output:
listen / silent -> True
hello / world -> False
Dormitory / dirty room -> True
hint: Two words are anagrams if they contain the same letters, so their sorted letters match. Remove spaces with .replace(" ", "") first.

title: Grade Calculator
prompt: Write letter(score) that returns A (90+), B (80+), C (70+), D (60+) or F. Print the grade for each student in {"Ana": 92, "Ben": 78, "Cleo": 85, "Dev": 64}.
output:
Ana: A
Ben: C
Cleo: B
Dev: D
hint: Use if / elif / else, checking the highest grade first. Loop over the dictionary with .items() to get name and score together.

title: Caesar Cipher
prompt: Write caesar(text, shift) that shifts each letter by shift places, wrapping around the alphabet and keeping case and punctuation. Encrypt "Hello, World!" with shift 3, then decrypt it with -3.
hint: ord() turns a letter into a number and chr() turns it back. Subtract ord("a") (or ord("A")), add the shift, use % 26 to wrap, then add it back.

title: Two Sum
prompt: Write two_sum(nums, target) that returns the indexes of the two numbers that add up to target, as a tuple. Test ([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) and ([3, 2, 4], 6). Aim for one pass.
hint: As you loop, store each number's index in a dictionary. For each new number, check whether target - number is already in the dictionary.

title: Merge Sorted Lists
prompt: Without using sorted() or .sort(), merge [1, 4, 7, 10] and [2, 3, 8] into one sorted list.
hint: Keep an index into each list. Repeatedly take the smaller of the two current items. When one list runs out, add whatever is left of the other.
solution:
def merge(a, b):
    i = j = 0
    result = []
    while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
        if a[i] <= b[j]:
            result.append(a[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            result.append(b[j])
            j += 1
    result.extend(a[i:])
    result.extend(b[j:])
    return result


print(merge([1, 4, 7, 10], [2, 3, 8]))

title: Transpose a Matrix
prompt: Flip the rows and columns of [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]] so you get a 3×2 matrix. Try doing it with zip().
hint: zip(*matrix) unpacks the rows and pairs up their first items, then their second items, and so on. Each result is a tuple, so convert it with list().
solution:
matrix = [[1, 2, 3],
          [4, 5, 6]]

transposed = [list(row) for row in zip(*matrix)]
print(transposed)

title: Run-Length Encoding
prompt: Write rle(text) that compresses runs of repeated characters, so "aaabccdddd" becomes "a3b1c2d4".
hint: Remember the current character and how many times you've seen it in a row. When the character changes, save the pair and start a new count. Don't forget the last run.

title: Rotate a List
prompt: Write rotate(items, k) that moves every item k places to the right, wrapping around. Rotate [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] by 2, then by 7.
hint: Rotating by the list's length changes nothing, so start with k %= len(items). Then glue two slices together: the last k items followed by the rest.
solution:
def rotate(items, k):
    if not items:
        return items
    k %= len(items)
    return items[-k:] + items[:-k]


print(rotate([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2))
print(rotate([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 7))

title: Safe Division
prompt: Write safe_divide(a, b) using try/except. Return the result normally, "Cannot divide by zero" for a zero divisor, and "Invalid input" for wrong types. Test (10, 2), (5, 0) and ("10", 2).
output:
5.0
Cannot divide by zero
Invalid input
hint: Dividing by zero raises ZeroDivisionError, and dividing a string raises TypeError. You can have several except blocks, one per error type.

title: Balanced Brackets
prompt: Write is_balanced(s) that checks whether every (, [ and { is closed in the right order. Test "([]{})", "([)]", "((" and "{[()()]}".
hint: Use a list as a stack. Push opening brackets. On a closing bracket, pop and check it matches. At the end, the stack must be empty.

title: Binary Search
prompt: Write binary_search(items, target) for a sorted list that returns the index or -1. Search [3, 8, 15, 21, 34, 42, 57, 66] for 34 and for 10.
hint: Keep lo and hi. Look at mid = (lo + hi) // 2. If it's too small move lo up past it, if too big move hi down. Stop when lo > hi.

title: Flatten a Nested List
prompt: Write flatten(items) that turns [1, [2, [3, 4], 5], [6], 7] into a flat list, however deep the nesting goes.
hint: This is a natural fit for recursion. isinstance(item, list) tells you whether to dig deeper or just append the item.

title: Fibonacci Generator
prompt: Write a generator function fib(n) that yields the first n Fibonacci numbers (0, 1, 1, 2, ...). Print list(fib(10)).
hint: A function with yield instead of return becomes a generator: it pauses after each yield and resumes on the next request. Swap values with a, b = b, a + b.

title: Pascal's Triangle
prompt: Write pascal(rows) that returns the first rows of Pascal's triangle as a list of lists. Print the first 5 rows, one per line.
hint: Each row starts and ends with 1. Every number in between is the sum of the two numbers above it in the previous row.

title: Group Anagrams
prompt: Write group_anagrams(words) that groups words made of the same letters. Test ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]. Keep groups in the order they first appear.
hint: Words that are anagrams have the same sorted letters, so "".join(sorted(word)) makes a perfect dictionary key. dict.setdefault(key, []) creates the list on first use.

title: Bank Account Class
prompt: Create a BankAccount class with an owner, a balance, and deposit() / withdraw() methods. withdraw() should raise ValueError("Insufficient funds") if there isn't enough money. Deposit 100, withdraw 30, then try to withdraw 500.
hint: __init__ sets up self.owner and self.balance. Use raise ValueError("...") inside the method, and catch it outside with try / except ValueError as e.
